# Data Processing {#sec-walker-data-importing}

```{r}
#| label: silent-packages
#| include: false

options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"))

library(here)
```

The goal of this is a single dataframe that will be saved in a folder (I use `data\saved data`) that can be imported at the beginning of the analysis scripts. More on that later.

Data processing has three main steps — merge the data, create the variables, and clean the data — that are done with code written in scripts. So, make a folder in scripts called **data processing** and open a new R script.

I'm not going to assume you know anything about R, so I'll use this step to introduce some key ideas and concepts.

One of the big challenges in writing scripts is *readability*. You want to write something that a human can understand as easily as possible. Two little habits that go a very, very long way are sections and comments. Both rely on `#`, which tells the machine to ignore whatever follows on that line.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Coding Practices: Sections and Comments"}
Sections are labeled blocks in scripts.

Create a section by starting a line with `#` and ending it with four or more dashes or equals signs.

`# section example 1----`

`#==== SECTION EXAMPLE 2 ====`

You can run all the code in a section (Code → Run Region → Run Code Section), fold/collapse a section, and jump to section headers using the pane between your script and the console.

Within sections, use (lots of) comments to explain the code in detail.

`# create the women's share of applicants variable`
:::

## Import US News & World Report Ranking

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Coding Learning Objectives

- `here()`
- `pacman::p_load()`
:::

Let's start with a simple task: import a single Excel file, the U.S. News & World Report ranking.

The easiest way to import a file is to navigate to it in the *Files* pane of Rstudio and click on it. Rstudio will offer to import the data for you, but that's not reproducible. Instead, copy the code it generates and paste it into your script.

```{r}
#| label: import-error-rankings
#| error: true
df.rank <- read_excel("data/original data/USNWR.xlsx")
```

Get used to errors. They happen a lot. Fortunately, you can paste error messages into a low-grade AI model and it can usually interpret it for you. This error is saying it doesn't know the function `read_excel()`. That's because we didn't load the package first. Out of the box, R doesn't have a lot of functionality – this is intentional – but you can add functionality with packages which, very broadly, is a set of cohesive functions. Let's do that now. We will install and add the package.

This is an excellent place to add sections and comments.

```{r}
#| label: workflow-rankings-initial
#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
suppressMessages(install.packages("readxl", quiet = TRUE))
library(readxl)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
df.rank <- read_excel("data/original data/USNWR.xlsx")
```

That works, but the path is fragile. It's typed out exactly as it sits relative to wherever R's working directory happens to be right now, which depends on how you opened R, not on where your files actually live. Move the script, hand it to a classmate, or open R a different way, and `"data/original data/USNWR.xlsx"` may no longer point anywhere real.

This is best solved with the `here()` function from the *here* package. It constructs paths starting from the location of your `.Rproj` file, which is very complementary to Projects (see @sec-projects) — since that file marks a fixed home base, `here()` always knows where "home" is regardless of how R was launched. You'll get a message about this when you load the package. Make sure it's not already loaded with `detach("package:here", unload = TRUE)` -- it's ok if this throws an error. Then, load it with `library(here)`. You'll get a message in your console telling you where it "starts". Test this by typing `here()` into your console.

When you add text as an argument to `here()` it adds it into the path so that `here("data")` creates a path to the *data* folder, which should already exist. These paths can be stored as variables and used as arguments for the `here()` function.

::: {.callout-tip title="Coding Practices: here()"}
Construct file paths with the `here()` function instead of verbatim.

```{r}
#| label: demo-here
#| eval: false
#don't do this
rankings.path <- "data/original data/USNWR.xlsx"

#use here() instead
rankings.path <- here("data","original data","USNWR.xlsx")

#even better
data.path <- here("data","original data")
rankings.path <- here(data.path,"USNWR.xlsx")
```
:::

Let's include this in our workflow.

```{r}
#| label: workflow-rankings-here
#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
suppressMessages(install.packages("readxl", quiet = TRUE))
library(readxl)

suppressMessages(install.packages("here", quiet = TRUE))
library(here)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))
```

The *LOAD PACKAGES* section is getting a little heavy. It installs the packages every time, and we really should have those lines for reproducibility, and it's starting to take up some vertical space. One thing we can do to help with this is a package helper package called *pacman*. It has a function called `p_load` that combines installing and loading into one step and accepts multiple packages as arguments. you have to install it with the typical method, but after that we can streamline the *LOAD PACKAGES* section.

```{r}
#| label: demo-pacman
#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))
```

You can examine the dataframe with `view(df.rank)` or by clicking on it in the Data frame in the upper right of Rstudio.

## Import Application Data

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Coding Learning Objectives

- pipe operator: `|>`
- `mutate()`
- `bind_rows()`
- `for` loop construction
:::

Now let's bring in something a little more involved: the applications data, which is split across one file per year instead of a single spreadsheet.

Start with the same technique as before. Navigate to the file in the *Files* pane in the lower right side of Rstudio and click on the file you wish to import.

```{r}
#| label: import-error
#| error: true

#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))

#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====
df <- read_csv("data/original data/IPEDS/ADM/adm2018_rv.csv")
```

Same error as before, same fix — `read_csv()` lives in `readr`, which is attached to the workhorse of data-wrangling , tidyverse [@wickham2019tidyverse]. Tidyverse is actually a collection of R packages — including `readr`, `dplyr`, and `purrr` — built around a shared philosophy of tidy data. Load it once at the top of your script with `library(tidyverse)`. In fact, the *readxl* package is installed with *tidyverse,* but doesn't get attached automatically.

Loading the *tidyverse* package with `pacman::p_load()` should stop the error. Additionally, we can use `here()` to generate a path to the *ADM* folder building from `data.path` which points to the *original data* folder.

```{r}
#| label: workflow-tidyverse
#| error: true

#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#auto installs:ggplot2, tibble, tidyr, readr, purrr, dplyr, stringr, forcats
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))

#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====
#build ADM folder path
folder.path <- here(data.path,"IPEDS","ADM")
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,"adm2018_rv.csv"))
```

You can have a look at the dataframe with `view(df)` or by clicking on it in the Environment pane in the upper right of Rstudio. It has `r nrow(df)` rows and `r ncol(df)` columns. The sheer width of it makes it difficult to find the variables of interest. So, instead we just ask for the names of the variable in the console:

```{r}
#| label: demo-names
names(df)
```

It might be easier to read the variables if they were in some order.

```{r}
#| label: demo-sort-names
sort(names(df))
```

Ok! So, this dataframe contains what we need! It has

- UNITID, which identifies the school

- APPLCNM, the number of men applicants

- APPLCNW, the number of women applicants

Before moving forward, notice the nesting in `sort(names(df))`. With more complicated code, nesting hampers readability so you'll want to use the pipe operator: `|>`. Then, instead of reading inside-out, you read left to right.

::: {.callout-tip title="Coding Practices: Pipe Operator"}
The pipe operator places the left-hand side into the *first* slot of the right-hand function.

```{r}
#| label: demo-pipe
#| eval: false

sort(names(df))
df |> names() |> sort()
```

The shortcuts are:

- **Windows/Linux:** `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `M`
- **Mac:** `Cmd` + `Shift` + `M`
:::

Returning to the variables in the data, we have UNITID, APPLCNM, APPLCNW, but we don't have the year. We need to make a new variable that has the year. More basically, we need to make a new variable from existing variables, which is to say **mutate** it from existing variables. You can do that with the `mutate()` function from the *tidyverse* package.

::: {.callout-tip title="Coding Practices: `mutate()`"}
mutate() creates a new variable by applying functions existing variables.
:::

```{r}
#| label: workflow-year
#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#auto installs:ggplot2, tibble, tidyr, readr, purrr, dplyr, stringr, forcats
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))

#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====
#build ADM folder path
folder.path <- here(data.path,"IPEDS","ADM")

#read files
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,"adm2018_rv.csv")) |> mutate(year = 2018)
```

Now, let's bring in the next file. We can copy and paste the code and just change the year.

```{r}
#| label: workflow-copypaste-1
##==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#auto installs:ggplot2, tibble, tidyr, readr, purrr, dplyr, stringr, forcats
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))

#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====
#build ADM folder path
folder.path <- here(data.path,"IPEDS","ADM")

#read files and add year variable
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,"adm2018_rv.csv")) |> mutate(year = 2018)
df2 <- read_csv(here(folder.path,"adm2019_rv.csv")) |> mutate(year = 2019)
```

Now, we need to combine them. *If* the data have all the same columns – which they should in this particular instance – then you simply want to stack them (bind the rows together). Just for fun, I'm going to ask AI how to do this. I'll copy and paste my code into Google and ask it how to combine the data.

![Asking an AI overview how to combine two years of data with `bind_rows()`](images/bind-rows.png){width="544"}

It, correctly, suggests `bind_rows()`. Not to be too trusting, you quickly verify by typing in the console `?bind_rows()` which brings up the documentation. It seems legit so now we can consolidate. Now,

```{r}
#| label: workflow-bindrows
#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#auto installs:ggplot2, tibble, tidyr, readr, purrr, dplyr, stringr, forcats
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))

#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====
#build ADM folder path
folder.path <- here(data.path,"IPEDS","ADM")

#read files and add year variable
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,"adm2018_rv.csv")) |> mutate(year = 2018)
df2 <- read_csv(here(folder.path,"adm2019_rv.csv")) |> mutate(year = 2019)

#combine dataframes
df <- df |> bind_rows(df2)
```

Let's do the next file. We copy and paste the df2 line, change the filename and the year, and then repeat binding in the last line.

```{r}
#| label: workflow-copypaste2
#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#auto installs:ggplot2, tibble, tidyr, readr, purrr, dplyr, stringr, forcats
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))

#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====
#build ADM folder path
folder.path <- here(data.path,"IPEDS","ADM")

#read files and add year variable
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,"adm2018_rv.csv")) |> mutate(year = 2018)
df2 <- read_csv(here(folder.path,"adm2019_rv.csv")) |> mutate(year = 2019)

#combine dataframes
df <- df |> bind_rows(df2)

#combine dataframes
df <- df |> bind_rows(df2)

#overwrite df2 with next file (fine since that info is in df)
df2 <- read_csv(here(folder.path,"adm2020_rv.csv")) |> mutate(year = 2020) #correct filename and year

#add to existing dataframe
df <- df |> bind_rows(df2)
```

We could continue copying and pasting, but....

::: {.callout-tip title="Coding Tip: Always be Automating"}
Replaced repeated processes with automation.
:::

Now that we understand our process, let's try to automate it. The process is

- use the filename and `here()` to construct the path
- import the file
- add the year
- add it to the previously imported data
- repeat for each file in the folder

Let's start by getting a list of the names of all the files in the directory. R provides a convenient function for this `list.files()`.

```{r}
#| label: demo-listfiles

folder.path <- here(data.path,"IPEDS","ADM")

#get list of files in ADM folder
lf <- list.files(folder.path)

#show list of files
lf
```

We've got the list and stored it as a value. You can access specific entries from the list by their numerical place. The first item on the list is `lf[1]` –\> `r lf[1]`. The third, fourth, and fifth items are `lf[3:5]` –\> `r lf[3:5]`

This means we can construct a file path using the list.

```{r}
#| label: demo-filepath
#| eval: false

folder.path <- here("data","original data","IPEDS","ADM")
lf <- list.files(folder.path)

#construct path to first file in folder
here(folder.path,lf[1])
```

So, we can import the first file in the folder by simply using its numerical place in the list.

```{r}
#| label: workflow-indexpath
#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#auto installs:ggplot2, tibble, tidyr, readr, purrr, dplyr, stringr, forcats
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))

#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====
#build ADM folder path
folder.path <- here(data.path,"IPEDS","ADM")

#get list of files in ADM folder
lf <- list.files(folder.path)

#read files and add year variable
##index variable
ll <- 1
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll]))
```

Next, we need to automate adding the year variable. Fortunately, it's contained in the file name. We just need to extract the four-digit year sequence from the name – which is stored in R as a string (that's just what it's called). There are a handful of ways to do this (so AI will give you a few recommendations), but you're probably better off using the *tidyverse* method: `str_extract()`. Working with strings is a thing in and of itself and well beyond the scope of what we need to understand. So, it doesn't make a lot of sense (at first blush) why this work, but it does.

```{r}
#| label: demo-str_extract()
#extract four digit sequence
lf[1] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+")
```

Add this to our workflow.

```{r}
#| label: workflow-autoyear
#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#auto installs:ggplot2, tibble, tidyr, readr, purrr, dplyr, stringr, forcats
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))

#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====
#build ADM folder path
folder.path <- here(data.path,"IPEDS","ADM")

#get list of files in ADM folder
lf <- list.files(folder.path)

#read files and add year variable
##index variable
ll <- 1
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll])) |> 
  mutate(year = lf[ll] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+"))
```

Again, we could copy and paste this for each file in the folder and just move the index variable forward every time so the next lines would be

```{r}
#| label: workflow-index2
#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#auto installs:ggplot2, tibble, tidyr, readr, purrr, dplyr, stringr, forcats
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))

#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====
#build ADM folder path
folder.path <- here(data.path,"IPEDS","ADM")

#get list of files in ADM folder
lf <- list.files(folder.path)

#read files and add year variable
##index variable
ll <- 1
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll])) |> 
  mutate(year = lf[ll] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+"))

##index variable
ll <- 2
df2 <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll])) |>
  mutate(year = lf[ll] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+"))

df <- df |> bind_rows(df2)
```

We could continue with the copy/paste, but let's try to Always be Automating, and use a `for` loop instead. It works like this

- for each item in a sequence – (item in seq)

- do stuff – {stuff}

The sequence that we want is the second, third, fourth, etc. item in the list of files. There are `r length(lf)` items in the folder, but rather than hard-code the value, we can access the number of items by asking the length of the list: `length(lf)`.

```{r}
#| label: workflow-loop
#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#auto installs:ggplot2, tibble, tidyr, readr, purrr, dplyr, stringr, forcats
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))

#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====
#build ADM folder path
folder.path <- here(data.path,"IPEDS","ADM")

#get list of files in ADM folder
lf <- list.files(folder.path)

#read files and add year variable
##initialize dataframe
ll <- 1
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll])) |> 
  mutate(year = lf[ll] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+"))

##loop over remaining files
for (ll in 2:length(lf)){
  #read file and add year variable
  df2 <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll])) |>
    mutate(year = lf[ll] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+"))

  #bind to exisiting dataframe
  df <- df |> bind_rows(df2)
}
```

## Check Application Data Import

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Coding Learning Objectives

- `select()`
- `datasummary_skim()`
:::

We seem to have successfully imported the applications data! More importantly, we have a ready made workflow that can be re-used for the directory data. However, were there to be an error in the initial workflow that was unnoticed, we would compound the mistake by blithely re-using it. It is, in fact, quite rare for a first pass to be mistake free so the wise coder pauses frequently to check imported data. Very frequently. There are a variety of checks that can (and should) be implemented, but the easiest one is in the *modelsummary* package.

So, load the package with `library(modelsummary)` (you may need to install it first with `install.packages("modelsummary")`). Then, use datasummary_skim(df) to examine your dataframe. That does turn out to be A LOT. So, let's focus on the variables of interest instead. That is, we'd like to select just a few columns from the dataframe to be "skimmed".

Quickly, `select()` is a *tidyverse* function that keeps only the listed columns from a dataframe and keeps them in the order they appear inside of `select()`. So, if a `df` has columns *a, b, c, ..., x, y, z*, `df |> select(z,x,y)` keeps only the last three columns and puts *z* first. For funsies, you could also do `df |> select(x,y,z) |> relocate(z)`.

```{r}
#| label: demo-datasummary_skim
library(modelsummary)
df |> select(UNITID,year,APPLCNM,APPLCNW) |> datasummary_skim()

```

Let's briefly discus what the "skim" shows.

UNITID is the unique indicator for a school. We see there are `r df |> distinct(UNITID) |> nrow()` schools in the sample. Since this, more or less, includes any school a person might attend after high school (post-secondary) – from clown college to medical school – it's seems reasonable. We have 0% missing school indicators which means every unit in the sample is identified.

APPLCNM is the number of men applicants to a school. We have a value for APPLCNM for each school in each year (I'll refer to this as school-year) as we have 0% missing. The mean value across the sample is `r mean(df$APPLCNM)` though the median is `r median(df$APPLCNM)`. This is exactly what we'd expect. A handful of huge public universities have applicant pools in the tens of thousands, which yanks the mean up without moving the median much. Indeed, the the highest observed value is `r max(df$APPLCNM)`, and the histogram shows the vast majority of the schools have very few male applicants (the lump on the left) but quite a few have very large values (the spread on the right).

This pattern is similar of for APPLCNW, the number of women applicants. The *year* variable has entries for `r min(df$year)`- `r max(df$year)`. The number of schools reporting in a year declines slightly, but the loss of `r df |> ungroup() |> group_by(year) |> summarize(n = n_distinct(UNITID)) |> pull(n) |> range() |> diff()` seems reasonably attributable to schools closing.

Nothing in this screams red flag, so we can proceed.

## Import Directory Data

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Coding Learning Objectives

- `filter()`
- `!`
:::

We can re-use our loop to import the directory data which contains, among other information, the school name and the state in which it is located. This last part is required to match schools to state policy.

We can start by renaming the final dataframe so we can overwrite `df`. Right after the `for` loop, we add `df.adm <- df`. The initial workflow created a few other variables that are no longer needed. As such, they can be removed from the environment with `rm()`, and we'll do this after the rename with `rm(folder.path,lf,ll,df,df2).`Now we can copy and paste everything from the `#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====` section down and re-use it for the *HD* data. We'll need to make only three minor changes:

1.  change the section and comments to indicate *HD*

2.  change the folder path to point the the *HD* folder

3.  rename the final dataframe to avoid overwriting `df.adm`

```{r}
#| label: workflow-hd
#==== LOAD PACKAGES =====
#load pacman to facilitate package loading
suppressMessages(install.packages("pacman",quiet = TRUE)) #do this quietly to suppress installation messages
library(pacman)

#load other packages
pacman::p_load(readxl,here)

#auto installs:ggplot2, tibble, tidyr, readr, purrr, dplyr, stringr, forcats
pacman::p_load(tidyverse)

#==== IMPORT RANKINGS DATA ====
#set original data folder path
data.path <- here("data","original data")
df.rank <- read_excel(here(data.path, "USNWR.xlsx"))

#==== IMPORT ADM DATA ====
#build ADM folder path
folder.path <- here(data.path,"IPEDS","ADM")

#get list of files in ADM folder
lf <- list.files(folder.path)

#read files and add year variable
##initialize dataframe
ll <- 1
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll])) |> 
  mutate(year = lf[ll] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+"))

##loop over remaining files
for (ll in 2:length(lf)){
  #read file and add year variable
  df2 <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll])) |>
    mutate(year = lf[ll] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+"))
  
  #bind to exisiting dataframe
  df <- df |> bind_rows(df2)
}

df.adm <- df
rm(folder.path,lf,ll,df,df2)

#==== IMPORT HD DATA ====
#set HD file path
folder.path <- here("data","original data","IPEDS","HD")

#get list of files in HD folder
lf <- list.files(folder.path)

##initialize dataframe
ll <- 1
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll])) |>
  mutate(year = lf[ll] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+"))

##loop over remaining files
for (ll in 2:length(lf)){
  #read file and add year variable
  df2 <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll])) |>
    mutate(year = lf[ll] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+"))
  
  #bind to exisiting dataframe
  df <- df |> bind_rows(df2)
}

df.hd <- df
rm(folder.path,lf,ll,df,df2)
```

This dataframe has `r nrow(df.hd)` observations, but we were expecting something much closer to `r nrow(df.adm)`. One way to investigate this is to get the list of units in `df.hd` that are not in `df.adm`. We can examine those schools for similarities or ask (Google/AI) why they aren't in the *ADM* survey.

```{r}
#| label: hd-latin1-encoding
#| include: false
#==== IMPORT HD DATA ====
#set HD file path
folder.path <- here("data","original data","IPEDS","HD")

#get list of files in HD folder
lf <- list.files(folder.path)

##initialize dataframe
ll <- 1
df <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll]), locale = locale(encoding ="Latin1")) |>
  mutate(year = lf[ll] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+"))

##loop over remaining files
for (ll in 2:length(lf)){
  #read file and add year variable
  df2 <- read_csv(here(folder.path,lf[ll]),locale = locale(encoding ="Latin1")) |>
    mutate(year = lf[ll] |> str_extract("\\d{4}+"))
  
  #bind to exisiting dataframe
  df <- df |> bind_rows(df2)
}

df.hd <- df
rm(folder.path,lf,ll,df,df2)
```

We can, and should, also "skim" the important variables in the dataframe.

```{r}
#| label: skim-df.hd

df.hd |> select(UNITID,year,STABBR) |> datasummary_skim()

```

No missing UNITIDs – great! Similar distribution of observations across the years in comparison to `df.adm`. The warning on the `STABBR` isn't great. That's an important variable and it didn't get "skimmed". Let's try counting the observations by state

```{r}
#| label: demo-count
df.hd |> count(STABBR) |> print(n=Inf)
```

There are `r df.hd |> count(STABBR) |> nrow()` "states" in the sample despite the U.S. having less than that. Well, R has a nice built-in command that gives you the state abbreviations for the U.S. `state.abb`. We'd like to see if any of the "states" in `df.hd` are not in the 50 listed in `state.abb`. This is best handled by the `filter()` function from *tidyverse*, which filters in rows of a dataframe based on a criteria. First, we'll see if filtering `df.hd` based on inclusion in `state.abb` removes anything. This would mean that some observations are not in U.S. states. We can note the removal because the filtered dataframe will have a smaller number of rows.

```{r}
#| label: demo-filter
df.hd |> filter(STABBR %in% state.abb) |> nrow()
```

`df.hd` has `r df.hd |> nrow()` rows before but the filter reduces it to `r (df.hd |> filter(STABBR %in% state.abb) |> nrow())` and we've lost `r (df.hd |> nrow()) - (df.hd |> filter(STABBR %in% state.abb) |> nrow())` observations by dong this. Let's see what we've lost.

R's logical negation operator is `!` and it, more or less, flips a true/false evaluator. For example ask `x == 2` asks R: is x equal to 2? If x has a value (maybe assigned with `x <- 2`) then R will respond with `TRUE` or `FALSE`. If you want to ask the opposite – is x *not equal* to 2 – you use the logical negation, `x != 2`.

```{r}
#| label: demo-!
df.hd |> filter(!(STABBR %in% state.abb)) |>  count(STABBR) |> print(n=Inf)
```

This shows that we have `r df.hd |> filter(!(STABBR %in% state.abb)) |> count(STABBR) |> nrow()` "states" that are actually not U.S. states. It turns out, Puerto Rico has `r df.hd |> filter(STABBR == "PR") |> nrow()` schools. Who knew?

## Import State Policy Data

The final data is the state policy. @walker2023anticipatory writes

> We categorized the universities into three groups based on state laws regarding abortion from the New York Times abortion tracker as of June 2023 (The New York Times 2023).

Rather than track down that tracker, we can get the data from their Table 1. You can do it by hand or ask AI. The result should be a file that is importable with our current techniques. We can add another section to the bottom of our current workflow.

